meta.title: Should you internationalize your SaaS at launch?
meta.description: Internationalizing a SaaS at launch: how to weigh translation, technical complexity and acquisition against real demand.
meta.excerpt: Planning for internationalization can make sense, but translating into six languages from day one does not guarantee visibility or customers.
meta.coverAlt: Aerial view of illuminated city buildings at dusk.

content.text: When building a SaaS, offering several languages seems like a great idea. More languages means potentially more users, right?
That is what I thought while developing
Iconise
, my AI-assisted icon creation app.
So I prepared the application for six languages: French, English, German, Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese and Japanese.
But looking back, I find myself asking:
does a technically accessible feature necessarily make a good product decision?

sections.title: Internationalization has never been more accessible

content.text: With frameworks such as Next.js, libraries such as next-intl and AI-assisted translation tools, internationalizing an application has become relatively straightforward.
There is still work to do, of course: translations, error messages, emails, regional formats, testing… But the technical barriers have come down considerably.
The problem is that this ease can encourage us to build features without really questioning their value.
Just because we can do something quickly does not necessarily mean we should.

sections.title: On Iconise, the complexity went beyond translation

content.text: Iconise generates content using artificial intelligence. I therefore had to distinguish between two settings:

items.text: The interface language, chosen by the user.
The language of the generated content, associated with each project.

content.text: A French user can work on an application intended for the Japanese market without having to switch their entire interface to Japanese.
This distinction is useful for the user experience, but it adds complexity.
With six languages for each setting, that means
36 possible combinations
I checked twelve of them in an initial round of testing that still needed to be taken further.
And that is just one example. Every new feature also means maintaining translations and checking their consistency.

sections.title: Six languages does not mean six markets won

content.text: This is probably the most important point.
Translating your application into German does not mean German users will automatically discover it.
Even with localized URLs,
hreflang
tags and a multilingual sitemap, there is still work to do on SEO, acquisition and, above all, the value proposition.
You need to understand what users in each market are looking for, how to reach them and what might convince them to use the product.
Internationalization opens the door to new markets. It does not guarantee that you will find customers there.

sections.title: Measure demand rather than adding more languages

content.text: To assess whether this decision makes sense, I think we need to look beyond the number of languages available.
The journey looks more like a funnel than a simple switch:
A few indicators can be useful:

items.text: Traffic from the different language versions.
The percentage of users who actually start a project.
The conversion rate to paying customers.

content.text: By comparing these figures with the countries and languages involved, we can start to identify markets with real potential.
Of course, these numbers do not tell the whole story. They can show where users drop off, but not necessarily why.

sections.title: So, should you internationalize from the start?

content.text: My position is quite simple:
plan the technical foundations for internationalization from the start, but do not necessarily translate the entire application immediately.
Starting with one or two languages and expanding gradually as demand emerges can be a more reasonable strategy.
On the other hand, for a product that is naturally international, offering several languages at launch can be entirely justified.
So I do not consider my choice on Iconise a mistake. But I will need to measure its impact before I can say it was a good investment.
Ultimately, the question is not how many languages our application can support, but how many genuinely add value for users and the product.
What comes next needs to be measured.
